q: A product's German price changes from 4,900 to 5,900 cents. Last month's German orders must still show 4,900. How should order_lines be modelled?
options: Only a foreign key to product_prices, and join to read the price
Store the unit price and product name on the line when the order is placed
Keep a price_history view computed from today's prices
Store the price on the line and keep it in sync with product_prices through a trigger
explain: The price at order time is a different fact from today's price, so it is stored on the line as a snapshot. A foreign key alone, or a trigger that follows the catalogue, would rewrite the history of orders already placed.

q: On 1 million rows, why was the primary key index on uuidv7() smaller than the one on uuidv4() (30 MB against 38 MB)?
options: UUIDv7 values are stored in 12 bytes instead of 16, because the timestamp part is packed
PostgreSQL compresses UUIDv7 values in B-tree indexes
New values sort after older ones, so they are appended instead of splitting pages
UUIDv7 indexes are built as hash indexes, which store a 4-byte hash of each key
explain: Both are 16 bytes (pg_column_size returned 16). The first 48 bits of a v7 are a millisecond timestamp, so inserts arrive in order like a sequence; random v4 keys land anywhere and leave split pages partly empty.

q: Order numbers such as DE-2026-000042 are printed on invoices, and each country numbers its orders on its own sequence. Where does the number belong?
options: In a number column with UNIQUE (country_code, number), next to a technical primary key
It should be the primary key of orders
In a number column with UNIQUE (number)
Generated by the application only, with no constraint, because it is a display value
explain: A natural key is kept unique by a constraint while a stable technical key is what foreign keys point to. A global UNIQUE (number) would forbid France and Germany from both having order 42, and no constraint at all lets duplicates in under concurrency.

q: With the session in UTC, what does SELECT '2026-10-29 10:00:00+02'::timestamp return?
options: 2026-10-29 08:00:00, converted to UTC
An error, because timestamp does not accept an offset
2026-10-29 10:00:00+02, with the offset kept
2026-10-29 10:00:00, the offset silently ignored
explain: Measured: plain timestamp drops the offset without an error. The conversion to 08:00:00+00 is what timestamptz does, which is why instants should always be stored as timestamptz.

q: Order statuses are a PostgreSQL enum. Product wants to remove the obsolete value awaiting_transfer. What happens with ALTER TYPE order_status DROP VALUE 'awaiting_transfer'?
options: It works if no row uses the value
It fails with 0A000 dropping an enum value is not implemented
It works but rewrites every table that has a column of that type
It fails only inside a transaction
explain: Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: removing an enum value is not implemented at all, so you would recreate the type. That cost is why a CHECK or a lookup table is usually the better choice for a set that evolves.

q: An insert breaks the exclusion constraint that forbids overlapping prices for the same product and country. Which SQLSTATE does the error carry?
options: 23P01
23505
23514
23503
explain: Measured: 23P01 conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint, followed by the constraint name. 23505 is a unique violation, 23514 a check and 23503 a foreign key; a handler usually maps both 23505 and 23P01 to a 409.

q: orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers (id) has no ON DELETE clause. You delete a customer who still has orders. What happens?
options: The orders are deleted too
The orders stay, with customer_id set to NULL automatically
It fails with 23503, because the default is NO ACTION
It fails with 23001, because the default is RESTRICT
explain: Measured: the delete failed with 23503 and a detail saying the key "is still referenced" from the child table. 23001 is what an explicit RESTRICT returns; cascading or nulling only happens when you ask for it.

q: Customers are soft-deleted with deleted_at. An email must be unique among the live accounts of a brand, and a customer who closed their account must be able to sign up again. Which definition does that?
options: UNIQUE (tenant_id, email, deleted_at), so deleted rows no longer collide with live ones
UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)
A SELECT before each INSERT in the signup handler, inside a transaction
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON customers (tenant_id, lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
explain: The partial unique index only covers live rows (measured: signing up again succeeded, a second live account failed with 23505). Adding deleted_at to a UNIQUE looks right but lets two live duplicates in, because their NULLs are not equal; a SELECT-then-INSERT races.

q: You enable row-level security with a tenant policy on orders, then test as the role that owns the table: it still sees every brand's orders. Why?
options: The policy needs a WITH CHECK clause before it applies to SELECT queries
The table owner bypasses policies unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
RLS only applies to INSERT and UPDATE
The policy is cached per connection, so it only applies after a reconnect
explain: Measured: the owner role saw 3 rows, and 2 after FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. WITH CHECK governs which rows you may write; USING already filters reads. Superusers bypass even FORCE, so the API uses a dedicated non-owner role.

q: Which field of a payment webhook should become a real column rather than stay inside jsonb?
options: A nested object you only display in the admin's event detail page
The whole raw body, kept for replaying the event
The event type, used in every query that lists and filters events
Optional metadata that a few providers send
explain: Fields you filter on deserve a column: it gets a type, constraints and planner statistics (measured: a JSON field filter was estimated at 100 rows for 200 real ones, the column at exactly 200). Data stored and returned whole is what JSONB is good at.

q: A developer edits a Flyway migration file that has already run in production, to fix a typo in a comment. What happens on the next deploy?
options: validate fails: the file's checksum no longer matches the recorded one
Flyway reruns the edited migration
Nothing: comments are ignored when comparing files
Flyway applies only the difference between the edited file and the applied one
explain: Flyway stores a checksum (CRC32 for SQL files) of every applied migration, and its documentation says validation fails on a checksum difference. Any change counts, comments included, which is why applied migrations are never edited: you add a new one.

q: On PostgreSQL 18, which statement rewrites the 50-million-row orders table?
options: ADD COLUMN note text
ADD COLUMN currency text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'
ADD COLUMN created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()
explain: Measured with the table's file node: a volatile default must be computed per row, so the table is rewritten under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. A constant, or now() evaluated once per statement, is stored in the catalog, which has avoided the rewrite since PostgreSQL 11.

q: The API exposes customer ids generated with uuidv7() in referral links. A privacy review raises a concern. Which one is real?
options: Anyone can guess the next customer's id from the current one
UUIDv7 ids can collide across servers, so one customer may see another's account
The id reveals when the account was created, to the millisecond
The id contains the server's MAC address
explain: The first 48 bits of a v7 are its creation time in milliseconds, and uuid_extract_timestamp returned it exactly (it returns NULL for a v4). The remaining bits are random, so ids are not guessable; the MAC address belonged to UUIDv1.

q: An import of the German supplier's product CSV maps a column with an explicit cast. What does this query return when the source value is 'abcdef'?
options: abcde, silently truncated
An error 22001 value too long for type character varying(5)
abcdef, because the cast is only a hint
An error 23514 naming a check constraint
explain: Measured, and documented: an explicit cast to varchar(n) truncates without an error. The 22001 error only happens when a too-long value is stored into the column without a cast. A text column with a named CHECK never truncates.

q: The first version of orders stores total as double precision euros, and finance reports totals off by a cent. The shop now also sells in pounds and Swiss francs. Which target design would you ship?
options: Keep double precision and round in every report
total_cents bigint plus a currency column, computed with integers in TypeScript
The PostgreSQL money type, which is built for amounts and rounds to cents
real: fewer digits means fewer rounding errors on small amounts
explain: Binary floats cannot represent most decimal amounts (0.1 + 0.2 returned 0.30000000000000004). Integer minor units are exact; numeric would also be correct. The money type depends on lc_monetary and stores no currency.

q: What does this script leave in the table?
options: Both statements fail with 23505
Four rows: UNIQUE never compares NULL values, in either column
Statement 1 fails, statement 2 succeeds
Two rows: statement 1 succeeds, statement 2 fails with 23505
explain: Measured: a plain UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct, so column a accepted two NULLs; NULLS NOT DISTINCT on b rejected the second NULL with Key (b)=(null) already exists, and the whole second statement was rolled back.

q: Two admins save a German price for the same product at the same moment. The admin service checks for overlapping validity periods with a SELECT before inserting. Sometimes both get in. Which fix would you ship?
options: Add a unique index on (product_id, country_code, valid_during)
Retry the SELECT twice before inserting
An exclusion constraint on (product_id WITH =, country_code WITH =, valid_during WITH &&)
Run the check and the insert in a READ COMMITTED transaction with a retry
explain: The exclusion constraint is checked by Postgres atomically for every writer (measured: an overlapping insert failed with 23P01). A unique index on the range only rejects identical ranges, not overlapping ones, and check-then-insert races at the default isolation level (M09).

q: A foreign key is declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. In one transaction you delete the parent row, then its child rows, then commit. With which ON DELETE action does that succeed?
options: NO ACTION: the check waits until commit, when no child is left
RESTRICT: it is the deferrable variant of NO ACTION
Both: deferral applies to every action
Neither: deleting a referenced parent always fails at once, deferred or not
explain: Measured: with NO ACTION deferred, the transaction committed. RESTRICT is checked immediately and is never deferred, which is the one real difference between the two refusals.

q: A cleanup job deletes customer accounts that never ordered, and each delete gets slower as orders grows. Every table has a primary key, and orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers (id). What is missing?
options: A unique index on customers.id
An index on orders.customer_id, which Postgres never creates for you
ON DELETE CASCADE, which makes the reference check go through an index
An ANALYZE on customers
explain: Measured: after creating a foreign key, pg_indexes showed only the table's primary key. The referenced side is already indexed by its primary key; each delete of a customer must look for referencing orders, which needs an index on customer_id.

q: The audit trigger on product_prices stores current_setting('app.user_id', true) as the author. A nightly price import, on a connection where an earlier transaction had set app.user_id locally, updates prices without setting it. What is recorded as the author?
options: NULL, because the second argument returns NULL for a missing setting
The user id of the earlier transaction
The update fails with 42704 unrecognized configuration parameter
An empty string
explain: Measured: once a transaction-local value has ended, the setting still exists on that connection and reads back as '', so the log recorded an empty author. NULL is only returned when the setting was never defined; wrap it in nullif(…, '').

q: The API role app_user runs this on a fresh connection, with the RLS policy USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint) on orders. What happens?
code:
SET ROLE app_user;
SELECT count(*) FROM orders;   -- no set_config before it
options: It returns the count of all orders
It returns 0
It fails with 42704 unrecognized configuration parameter "app.tenant_id"
It returns the count for the tenant most recently set by another session on the server
explain: Measured: without the two-argument form, current_setting raises an error when the setting does not exist, so the query fails closed. Returning 0 would require current_setting(…, true), which yields NULL and matches no row.

q: How do you make it impossible, at the schema level, for an order line of tenant 2 to point to an order of tenant 1?
options: A UNIQUE (tenant_id, id) on orders, and lines referencing orders (tenant_id, id)
Add a CHECK (tenant_id = order_id) on lines
Use UUIDs for order ids, so that no tenant can guess an id belonging to another tenant
Add an index on order_lines (tenant_id, order_id)
explain: A composite foreign key carries the tenant into the reference (measured: the cross-tenant insert failed with 23503 … Key (tenant_id, order_id)=(2, 1) is not present). Unguessable ids reduce the risk but do not stop a bug that copies the wrong id; an index enforces nothing.

q: The group plans to host white-label shops for 5,000 small merchants on the Orders API, each a tenant, and ships schema changes weekly. A colleague proposes one PostgreSQL schema per tenant "for isolation". What do you answer?
options: Agree: schemas cost nothing and isolate data completely
Shared tables with tenant_id and RLS; per-schema means 5,000 migration runs a week
Prefer one database per tenant, which is simpler to operate than thousands of schemas
Agree, but only if each schema has its own connection pool
explain: Schema per tenant runs every migration once per schema, 5,000 times a week here, and grows the catalog with each schema; it suits a small number of large tenants. Database per tenant is the most expensive to operate and is kept for contractual isolation or residency.

q: On PostgreSQL 18, you promote a hot JSON field and then index it. The second statement fails. Why, and what would you do?
options: ->> is not immutable; use -> instead
Generated columns cannot reference jsonb; copy the field into a plain column with a trigger
The column needs NOT NULL before it can be indexed
Generated columns are virtual by default in PostgreSQL 18; index the expression instead
explain: Measured: the column was created as virtual and the index failed with 0A000 indexes on virtual generated columns are not supported. An expression index on (payload ->> 'kind') works without touching the table; a STORED column would also work but rewrites the table when added.

q: A node-pg-migrate migration contains only CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on orders. The deploy fails with 25001. What is the fix?
options: Remove CONCURRENTLY: inside a migration the write lock does not matter much
Wrap the statement in an explicit BEGIN / COMMIT
Call pgm.noTransaction() and drop any leftover invalid index first
Run the migration with a superuser role
explain: node-pg-migrate runs pending migrations in one transaction by default, and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY failed with 25001 cannot run inside a transaction block. A plain CREATE INDEX would block writes for the whole build; a role change does not affect transactions.

q: You need a public_id uuid filled for every row of the live orders table, without a long lock. Which sequence would you ship?
options: ADD COLUMN public_id uuid, then SET DEFAULT uuidv7(), then backfill in batches
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7() in a single statement, run at night when traffic is low
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT uuidv7() with lock_timeout set
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid GENERATED ALWAYS AS (uuidv7()) STORED
explain: Measured: adding the column and then setting the default caused no rewrite, new rows got an id, existing rows stayed NULL for the backfill. A volatile default in ADD COLUMN rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and lock_timeout only limits the wait for the lock, not the rewrite.

q: After a complete backfill, how do you make orders.total_cents NOT NULL on the busy 50-million-row table?
options: ALTER COLUMN total_cents SET NOT NULL with lock_timeout = '3s'
ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK (total_cents IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, then SET NOT NULL
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on total_cents, then SET NOT NULL
ALTER COLUMN total_cents SET DEFAULT 0, which turns existing NULLs into zeros and forbids new ones
explain: Validation scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue, and the final SET NOT NULL reported that existing constraints prove the column has no NULLs instead of scanning. A plain SET NOT NULL scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; lock_timeout bounds the wait, not the scan.

q: A migration runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text, a catalog-only change. Yet the API stops answering for two minutes. What most likely happened?
options: Adding a column rewrote the table
The new column invalidated every index on the table
The migration tool held its advisory lock for two minutes, blocking the application's own queries
The ALTER queued behind a long transaction, and every query on the table queued behind the ALTER
explain: A waiting lock request blocks later conflicting requests too (the PostgreSQL docs call it a soft block, ahead in the wait queue). The fix is SET lock_timeout in migrations, whose default is 0 (wait forever), plus a retry. Adding a nullable column measured no rewrite.

q: A backfill picks each batch with the first query. Halfway through, it is much slower than at the start. What explains it?
options: The IS NULL filter cannot use any index, so every batch reads the whole table from disk
The updated rows are still locked by earlier batches, so the query waits for them
It rescans every row already filled: 1,182 buffers against 10 for the keyset query
LIMIT forces a sort of the whole table
explain: Measured with 90,000 of 100,000 rows done: the plan used the primary key index but showed Rows Removed by Filter: 90000 and 1,182 buffers; the keyset version read 10. Each batch gets slower, so the total cost grows with the square of the table.

q: For the UK launch you must rename orders.zip_code to orders.postal_code, with rolling deploys. Which plan is safe?
options: RENAME COLUMN in the migration, and deploy the code that uses postal_code in the same release
Add postal_code, sync and backfill it, switch reads then writes, drop zip_code later
Create a view named orders exposing both names, then rename the table
RENAME COLUMN at night, when no old instance is running
explain: During a rolling deploy, old instances still query zip_code, so an instant rename breaks them even though the rename itself is fast. Expand / migrate / contract keeps every intermediate schema compatible with both versions; relying on a night window is downtime with better timing.
